summary.text: 渴 combines a water-related component with a sound component. It commonly means “thirsty” or “parched”; an older use is reported for “exhausted” or “dried up.”

formation.text: 渴 is a phonosemantic compound: 氵 supplies a water-related meaning category, while 曷 is traditionally analyzed as a sound element. The early dictionary gloss “exhausted” is a historical interpretation, not proof of the graph’s prehistoric origin.

components.text: 氵 is the component form of 水 and contributes a water-related meaning category here. The bronze analysis describes 水; the sources do not provide a full graphic sequence from that form to the modern graph.
曷 is traditionally analyzed as the sound element in 渴. Part of its ancient bronze form has no secure identified referent; that uncertainty does not by itself rule out its sound role here.

sound_limitation.text: The supplied Old Chinese comparison shares final and coda material but has different initial reconstructions. This qualifies the sound comparison; it does not independently establish 曷’s role in 渴.

sound.text: The reconstructions share final and coda material but differ in their initials, so the comparison is qualified.
This system gives two reconstructions for 渴; the comparison remains qualified.
The modern Mandarin readings differ; this pair does not establish the ancient sound relation.

history.text: A character-specific account catalogs bronze, seal, and manuscript examples and analyzes a bronze form as 水 plus the sound element 曷. These examples do not establish a complete dated sequence.
An early dictionary analyzes 渴 as 从水、曷聲 and glosses it as “exhausted.” This is an early lexicographic account, not direct evidence of the graph’s earliest formation.

uncertainties.text: The cited analysis does not securely identify the original referent of the middle element in 曷’s bronze form. This does not by itself rule out 曷’s phonetic role in 渴.
氵 is identified as a component form of 水, but the sources do not provide a full graphic sequence showing how the form developed in 渴.

senses.text: A bronze use is interpreted as “drying up” or “exhausted,” with the graph reported as writing 竭. The Fanghu transcription itself prints 竭 and does not independently confirm the graph identification.

senses.period: Cited in 詩·王風·君子于役; earliest physical witness date unresolved
senses.text: A cited Shijing passage uses 渴 to mean “thirsty.” The date of the passage’s earliest surviving physical witness is unresolved.
A cited Tang usage has the sense “dry” or “parched.”
A cited 公羊傳 passage uses 渴 to mean “urgent”; its relation to the other senses is not established.

developments.text: A shift from “exhausted” or “dried up” to “thirsty” is plausible, but the intervening stages are not traced.

limitations.text: The bronze use is reported with the meaning “exhausted” or “dried up,” but is not securely established as the character’s original meaning. The earliest physical witness for the cited thirst passage is also unresolved.
The separate sense “urgent” is recorded, but its development or connection to the other senses is not established.

overview.text: 渴 combines a water-related component with a sound component. It commonly means “thirsty” or “parched”; an older use means “exhausted” or “dried up.”

曷 is analyzed as the sound element; historical comparisons make the match less straightforward.

relationships.text: 氵, a component form of 水, contributes the water-related meaning category in 渴.
曷 is traditionally analyzed as the phonetic element in 渴. The supplied Old Chinese reconstructions differ in their initials, so the proposed sound relation is qualified.
